summary: The machine has the tools and DocumentDB MCP server and agent skills required to build the Beanie + OpenAI cross‑sell sample against the live, vector-capable Azure DocumentDB cluster. Most cold-answer facts needed for coding were either verified or corrected from authoritative sources. Remaining gaps are non-blocking (embedding model choice, sample-size decisions, and a few local dev choices).
summary_points: All required run-time tools for building the sample (python, pip, node/npx, Docker, az) and the DocumentDB MCP server are available — the build can start now against the live cluster.

Many of the model's 'cold answers' were incorrect or outdated about the product surface: the right resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, cluster provisioning is vCore/tiered (M-series), connection URIs use mongodb+srv and may require mongodb+srv host suffixes, and vector/text indexes are created with DocumentDB's search APIs (cosmosSearch / createSearchIndexes).

Agent skills that the builder will want (documentdb-connection, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-azure-deployment, documentdb-mcp-setup, documentdb-driver, documentdb-full-text-search) are installed and available for guidance and verification.

Missing CLI tools (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet, mongosh) are present in inventory as not-on-PATH; none block building the sample against the provided live cluster, but installing mongosh would materially help manual verification.

Information gaps remain that the builder must decide (which OpenAI embedding model and exact vector dimension, seed-data size for index tuning, whether to show Entra-based auth in examples). These are not fatal but must be documented in the sample README.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for the account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource type name used in ARM/Bicep/Terraform).
confusions.grounded_answer: The current resource type for managed Azure DocumentDB clusters (vCore, new managed MongoDB clusters) is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts still exists for Cosmos DB database accounts (the legacy Cosmos DB databaseAccount resource), but vCore DocumentDB clusters use the mongoClusters resource type.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Same provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) historically used for Cosmos DB accounts (`databaseAccounts`), and older docs / examples that use `databaseAccounts` still exist; the newer vCore-managed MongoDB product adds `mongoClusters` as the resource type.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used ARM/Bicep/Terraform `databaseAccounts` to target a vCore DocumentDB cluster, deployments would fail or target the wrong resource type; any IaC included in the sample would be incorrect for vCore clusters.
improvements: On the Azure deployment quickstart / examples page (Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep), add a short note 'For vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (see example) — databaseAccounts is for Cosmos DB accounts.'
Update any sample IaC templates in the agent kit to default to `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters` where the sample targets vCore DocumentDB.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group `az cosmosdb`. Example to create a MongoDB-compatible account: `az cosmosdb create --name <ACCOUNT> ...`. The cosmosdb commands are part of the core Azure CLI (no separate extension required).
confusions.grounded_answer: The Azure CLI exposes commands for the mongoClusters resource under the `az cosmosdb mongocluster` subgroup (for example `az cosmosdb mongocluster create`). The `az cosmosdb` command group is the parent, but the cluster-specific subcommands are `az cosmosdb mongocluster ...`. Some preview features and tooling may also exist in `az documentdb` / `az cosmosdb` extension versions; check the installed CLI extensions if the command is not present.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The `az cosmosdb` group historically manages Cosmos DB database accounts (`databaseAccounts`) and examples often show `az cosmosdb create`. Newer cluster operations live under `az cosmosdb mongocluster` (or CLI extension/preview variants), so the cold answer omitted the cluster-specific subgroup.

confusion_sources.title: Older CosmosDB quickstarts that use `az cosmosdb create`

confusions.build_risk: Using the generic `az cosmosdb create` workflow would create a databaseAccounts/Cosmos account, not a vCore mongoClusters cluster — irrelevant to this sample (the prompt says use the provided cluster) but would mislead any IaC examples in the repo.
improvements: In the sample README and any deployment instructions, call out `az cosmosdb mongocluster` explicitly for cluster creation examples and state when `az cosmosdb create` targets a different resource type.
In the `documentdb-azure-deployment` skill docs, add CLI example snippets with the full `az cosmosdb mongocluster create` form and note extension/preview requirements.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type `Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts` (example API version `Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-07-01`). Terraform (azurerm): `azurerm_cosmosdb_account` for the account; use `azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database` / `azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection` for DB/collection resources on that account.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB clusters the correct ARM/Bicep resource type is `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters`. Terraform users should prefer the AzAPI/AzureRM resources that target the `mongoClusters` API (examples exist for azurerm_mongo_cluster / azapi usage and AVM modules). The `databaseAccounts` type remains valid for Cosmos DB database accounts (RU model) but not for vCore clusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Old/legacy Cosmos DB IaC examples use `databaseAccounts` and the Terraform azurerm provider has historically exposed `azurerm_cosmosdb_account`. The vCore product introduced `mongoClusters` as the dedicated resource type and newer AzAPI/Terraform modules target it.
confusions.build_risk: Including incorrect IaC in the sample (databaseAccounts) would create or target the wrong Azure resource; for this sample the build should NOT deploy the cluster, but any included IaC examples must reference mongoClusters where appropriate.
improvements: Update any CI / examples that show IaC to include `mongoClusters` examples and a one-liner comment describing the difference to `databaseAccounts`.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB API connection string for an Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB Mongo API) account: `mongodb://<USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>@<ACCOUNT_NAME>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<ACCOUNT_NAME>@`. TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true), port is 10255 (TLS endpoint).
confusions.grounded_answer: For modern Azure DocumentDB (vCore) clusters the published cluster connection string typically uses the SRV form (mongodb+srv) with the cluster host suffix such as `<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` and `tls=true`/`authMechanism` options. The older Cosmos DB Mongo API used `*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255` endpoints; that form still appears in Cosmos DB RU docs but DocumentDB (mongoClusters) uses `mongodb+srv://...global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` and may supply an explicit connection string from the portal (DOCUMENTDB_URI).

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The `mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255` form is correct for (legacy) Cosmos DB Mongo API accounts in many Microsoft docs and older quickstarts; newer vCore clusters and the DocumentDB product expose SRV (`mongodb+srv`) endpoints with `mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` hostnames. The two shapes look similar and share TLS/replica options but are distinct.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder hardcodes code to expect port 10255 and the older host suffix, driver connection may fail against the provided DOCUMENTDB_URI (which is likely a mongodb+srv SRV URI). The code must treat DOCUMENTDB_URI as an opaque URI and not assume host/port format.
improvements: In the sample README and examples, always show `DOCUMENTDB_URI` used as provided (don't assume port or host shape) and include a short note: 'Use the connection string from the portal / DOCUMENTDB_URI; vCore clusters publish mongodb+srv URIs.'

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed on Cosmos DB semantics: provisioned throughput expressed in Request Units (RUs/sec) or serverless (consumption) or autoscale RUs. For MongoDB API you typically choose provisioned RUs (or autoscale) or serverless where supported; there is not a traditional vCore compute-tier for the classic MongoDB API account (billing is RU-based or serverless).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore-managed clusters / mongoClusters) is a vCore/compute-tiered offering (M-series tiers such as M10, M20, M30 etc.) — capacity is provisioned in node tiers and storage dimensions, not in Cosmos DB Request Units (RUs). The RU model still applies to Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts) that use the RU billing model.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB's RU billing model is very prominent in older docs and covers the Cosmos RU-based Mongo API; the newer vCore DocumentDB clusters intentionally use vCore/compute tiers (M-series). The shared 'MongoDB compatibility' phrasing causes cross-mentioning in docs.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB docs describing RU billing and mongodb 10255 endpoints

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based billing they may pick wrong defaults for cluster sizing or suggest deploying RU autoscale in README; for this sample that only matters for guidance, not for code (the sample uses the provided cluster).
improvements: Add a short clarifying sentence in the top-level sample README: 'This sample targets an existing vCore Azure DocumentDB cluster (M-series). Do not confuse this with Cosmos DB RU-mode accounts.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane access for the MongoDB API is typically done with account credentials exposed as MongoDB username/password (the account primary/secondary keys or a database-scoped MongoDB user). Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) integration for the MongoDB API is not generally supported as a direct SASL/OAUTH mechanism — use the supplied MongoDB credentials.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) database users and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication. Entra ID auth is enabled per-cluster (`authConfig.allowedModes`), and clients can present Entra-issued OIDC tokens (MONGODB‑OIDC / MONGODB‑OIDC authMechanism) or use provider-specific flows; administrative Entra principals are manageable via ARM and non-administrative Entra identities via DB commands. The cluster can be configured to accept native and/or MicrosoftEntraID auth modes.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB Mongo API lacked Azure AD auth; the vCore DocumentDB product added Entra ID/OIDC support for cluster auth. Old Cosmos DB docs and older blog posts say Entra/AAD isn't supported, which is why models memorize the negative.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API docs and Q&A threads saying Entra/AAD is not supported

confusions.build_risk: If the builder promises only username/password auth in code examples, they might omit showing the Entra flow which some production customers will want to follow; sample must mention both options and read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env as instructed.
improvements: Add an example snippet in the sample's README showing how to switch between native connection-string auth and Entra/OIDC auth (link to the Entra auth doc).
In `documentdb-mcp-setup` and the sample README, document how to configure `authConfig.allowedModes` via az/ARM for Entra auth.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers. For Python async code use Motor (the async MongoDB driver) and an ODM such as Beanie (which is built on Motor + Pydantic). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB client SDK — you use the standard MongoDB driver for your language (pymongo/motor) pointed at the DocumentDB/Cosmos Mongo endpoint. For other Cosmos APIs there is `azure-cosmos`, but not for the MongoDB wire API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers. For async Python, Motor is the recommended driver and Beanie is a natural ODM on top of Motor; there is no separate DocumentDB-specific Mongo driver.
confusions.build_risk: None — this is the correct choice.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Newer MongoDB 7-style vector index types (HNSW, IVF, DiskANN) are exposed by the service as vector indexes on a field. Example (typical MongoDB command shape — service-specific options may vary): `db.product_pairs.createIndex({embedding: "vector"}, {name: "emb_idx", dimensions: 1536, algorithm: "hnsw", similarity: "cosine", efConstruction: 200, m: 16})`
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB's native vector index API is exposed via the `createSearchIndexes` command and the `$search` aggregation stage (engine `cosmosSearch`) with index subtypes `vector-diskann`, `vector-hnsw`, and `vector-ivf`. You should create a `cosmosSearch` vector index (e.g., `vector-diskann`) with the `dimensions` matching the embedding model and engine-specific options (lBuild/lSearch/maxDegree etc.). The exact DDL uses `createSearchIndexes`/`definition` rather than a vanilla `createIndex({embedding:'vector'})` call.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used the generic MongoDB 7-style `createIndex({field: 'vector'})` syntax (used by MongoDB 7+), but DocumentDB exposes vector indexing via its `createSearchIndexes`/`cosmosSearch` machinery and has service-specific options. The surface is similar (HNSW/DiskANN/IVF) so it's an easy mix-up.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create a vector index with the generic `createIndex` form, the command will fail or create an unsupported index; the sample must call the DocumentDB search index creation path.
improvements: Update any sample index creation snippets in the agent kit to use `createSearchIndexes` / `cosmosSearch` examples and include a short comment mapping DiskANN/HNSW/IVF to typical data-scale guidance.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: You can use MongoDB text indexes for basic full-text search via `db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'})` and `$text` queries. For richer semantic/hybrid search combine vector search (vector index) with text filtering client-side or via aggregation pipeline. For advanced language/semantic ranking integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or an external search service and combine results with vector-similarity results in the app.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB's recommended search route uses `createSearchIndexes` + the `$search` aggregation stage (BM25 scoring) and the service's `cosmosSearch` vector operator for hybrid search. The community `$text` operator and `{field:'text'}` text indexes are not the DocumentDB search path; instead use DocumentDB's search indexes and `$search` stage for full-text and hybrid (BM25 + vector) patterns (the skill documents Reciprocal Rank Fusion for hybrid).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Generic MongoDB advice often points to `text` indexes and `$text`. DocumentDB provides a richer built-in FTS pipeline (`createSearchIndexes` / `$search`) that the product docs and agent skills prefer.

confusion_sources.title: Generic MongoDB full-text doc examples (useful but not recommended here)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses `$text` / text indexes, it would miss BM25 scoring and the integrated vector search path; the sample must demonstrate `createSearchIndexes` / `$search` to show hybrid retrieval correctly.
improvements: Add canonical `$search` + `createSearchIndexes` examples to the agent kit and a short 'don't use `$text`' note on the top-level README.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported server/wire versions depend on the account configuration; modern accounts commonly advertise compatibility with MongoDB server versions (e.g., 5.0/6.0 and in newer accounts 7.0). However, the service is a compatibility layer atop Cosmos DB, so some MongoDB server features may be missing or limited: server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, and historically some change-stream/transaction semantics were limited. Always verify exact supported wire version and feature matrix for your account (the portal/az CLI or MCP tool will show the configured MongoDB server version).
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB has an explicit MongoDB compatibility matrix and supports multiple MongoDB wire versions (5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0 in newer APIs) and documents which aggregation operators and commands are supported or limited. The best practice is to consult the DocumentDB compatibility page for the exact server-version support and feature-level matrix. DocumentDB supports many features (including change streams / $changeStream in current versions), but some historical limitations remain documented.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: None if the builder consults the compatibility doc for any advanced feature; sample should avoid using esoteric, unverified server-side features.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator for the MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB account. Use the official MongoDB Docker image for local development: `docker run -d --name mongo-local -p 27017:27017 mongo:7.0` and connect to `mongodb://localhost:27017`. The Cosmos DB emulator (Windows) does not emulate the MongoDB API reliably; prefer a local MongoDB server for fast local tests and use the live DocumentDB cluster for final verification.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development there is a recommended Gateway Docker image (`ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest`) that exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). Use that gateway for local parity; a plain `mongo:7.0` image is not equivalent to the DocumentDB engine and will miss feature/compatibility differences.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Generic guidance for local MongoDB development (run mongo:latest) is common; the DocumentDB product provides a gateway image to emulate DocumentDB-specific behaviors and ports (10260) which is what the agent kit recommends.

confusion_sources.title: General MongoDB Docker image docs (not product-specific)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses plain MongoDB locally they may develop or test against features that differ from DocumentDB and then encounter issues at verification time; for correct parity use the DocumentDB gateway image or verify against the live cluster.
improvements: Add an explicit 'local development' section to the sample README showing how to run the DocumentDB gateway image (port 10260) and how to toggle between local gateway and live cluster via DOCUMENTDB_URI.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically the Cosmos DB MongoDB API did not fully support MongoDB change streams; instead Cosmos provides its own Change Feed feature (for SQL API) which can be used for data-change notifications. If you need change-stream-like capabilities against a MongoDB API account, either verify whether your account's MongoDB server version exposes change streams or use Cosmos DB's Change Feed for the account (which is a different API). There is not a universal 'enable change streams' toggle for the MongoDB API — check your cluster's feature support.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB currently supports `$changeStream` in its compatibility matrix for supported server versions, and the compatibility doc lists the `$changeStream` stage as supported in current versions. Always check the compatibility doc for your cluster server version; enabling Microsoft Entra ID or other cluster auth modes is independent from change-stream support.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (change stream support)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo accounts historically lacked full change-stream parity; many past posts and docs stated that change streams were unsupported. Newer DocumentDB versions/capabilities now include support; the model's memory reflected older state.

confusion_sources.title: Older Q&A threads and migration notes implying change-stream limitations

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are not available they might implement a more complex workaround; conversely relying on change streams without verifying the cluster's serverVersion could fail. The sample does not need change streams, so this is low risk.
improvements: Add a short note in the agent kit: 'Refer to the MQL compatibility matrix for whether `$changeStream` is available on your cluster's configured serverVersion.'

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the `documentdb` MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane tooling against a MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB cluster; the general Azure MCP server is focused on resource management and may not include the same data-plane inspection tools. The prompt indicates the `documentdb` MCP server's `default` profile is connected to the same cluster — use that for index inspection, query plans and data-plane diagnostics.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the `documentdb` MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, aggregate, explain_operation, etc.) tailored to DocumentDB clusters. The general `azure` MCP server is control-plane only and does not provide the same data-plane query/explain utilities.
confusions.build_risk: None — the inventory shows the documentdb MCP server is present and connected; the builder should call the data-plane tools through it.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had a service called Azure DocumentDB which was the precursor to Azure Cosmos DB. Azure Cosmos DB is the evolution / rebranding and multi-API superset; the MongoDB API is one of Cosmos DB's compatibility layers. The open-source 'DocumentDB' projects are separate and unrelated; the Azure names have changed over time, but today the managed service is Cosmos DB (DocumentDB namespace in ARM), and the MongoDB-compatible endpoint is a compatibility layer implemented by Microsoft on top of Cosmos DB's storage/engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but confused: There are multiple similarly named things. The original Azure DocumentDB (2014) was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. Separately, Microsoft released a vCore-based MongoDB-compatible offering that was previously called 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' then renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB' (the modern product). That modern Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (distinct from MongoDB) and is separate from Amazon DocumentDB and from Cosmos DB's RU-based accounts. The naming overlap is the root cause of confusion.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical renames and overlapping names (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB; a later vCore offering reusing 'DocumentDB' in its new name) cause models to conflate the original and modern services.

confusion_sources.title: FAQ note explaining the naming relationships

confusions.build_risk: Potential for inaccurate wording in the sample README that confuses users about which product is targeted; this is a documentation risk rather than a runtime risk.
improvements: Ensure the sample README uses the phrase 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore — MongoDB-compatible)' consistently and includes one short paragraph explaining how it differs from Cosmos DB (RU) and Amazon DocumentDB, with links to the FAQ page.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is the Cosmos DB proprietary distributed storage/engine exposing a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol. Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers but must expect some differences in behavior, supported commands, and performance characteristics (e.g., RU billing, potential limits on some aggregation stages or server-side JS).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the modern vCore product) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (Microsoft's DocumentDB project) which implements the MongoDB wire protocol compatibility. Applications should use standard MongoDB drivers, but must consult the compatibility matrix — there are subtle differences from MongoDB server and from Cosmos DB RU-model accounts, so test queries against the target cluster. The engine being DocumentDB (open-source) is important for license and multi-cloud portability reasons.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer attributed the cluster to Cosmos DB's proprietary engine; modern Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine and not the same as Cosmos DB RU internals. The similarity of user-facing APIs (Mongo protocol) led to the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Docs that mention DocumentDB engine and licensing

confusions.build_risk: Documentation and license statements in README could be wrong; but code using standard MongoDB drivers is unaffected.
improvements: Add a short 'engine & licensing' note in the README: 'Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine; you use MongoDB drivers but consult the compatibility matrix.'

confusions.question: Which database name will this sample create and use?
confusions.cold_answer: This sample will use the database named `sample_retail_19` for all created collections and indexes.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment (skill_md) explicitly instructs the sample to use `sample_retail_19`.
confusions.build_risk: None.

confusions.question: What vector index definition will the sample create for product-pair embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the `embedding` field of the product_pairs collection. Example DDL (subject to exact option names on the cluster): `db.product_pairs.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {name: 'emb_idx', dimensions: 1536, algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', efConstruction: 200, m: 16})`. Use the cluster's MCP tool to confirm exact index option names before creation.
confusions.grounded_answer: The sample should create a DocumentDB `createSearchIndexes` vector index (engine `cosmosSearch`) on the embedding field, specifying `dimensions` matching the embedding model and picking an index subtype (e.g., `vector-diskann` for larger datasets on M30+, or `vector-hnsw` for small datasets). The index DDL uses `createSearchIndexes` and `definition` blocks rather than a plain `createIndex` vector clause.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used MongoDB 7+ generic `createIndex({embedding:'vector'})` syntax; DocumentDB requires the `createSearchIndexes`/`cosmosSearch` index creation path.
confusions.build_risk: Index creation will fail if the sample uses the wrong index API. The sample must call the DocumentDB `createSearchIndexes` command with the correct index subtype and dimensions.
improvements: In the seed/index script included in the sample, use the MCP `createSearchIndexes` call (or show the exact driver-runCommand equivalent) and document the mapping from embedding model dims to `dimensions`.

confusions.question: How will the app authenticate to the cluster at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: The app will read the full MongoDB connection string from the environment variable `DOCUMENTDB_URI` and pass it unchanged to Motor/Beanie: e.g. `client = AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'])`. TLS must be accepted by the driver according to the connection string options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the run-environment requires the sample to read the cluster connection string from `DOCUMENTDB_URI` and use that with Motor/Beanie. The skill_md explicitly mandates this.
confusions.build_risk: Low — ensure the code does not log or commit the value and uses a .env.example with placeholders.

confusions.question: Which Python packages and install command will the sample use for Beanie + async Mongo?
confusions.cold_answer: Install with pip in the sample virtualenv: `pip install beanie motor pydantic[dotenv] openai python-dotenv`. Beanie runs on top of Motor (async pymongo) and Pydantic.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is correct and consistent with standard practice: use Motor as the async driver and Beanie as the ODM (plus openai/python-dotenv). Pin exact versions in requirements.txt during the build.
confusions.build_risk: None, but builder should pin versions and test compatibility (Beanie + Motor + Python version).
improvements: Add pinned versions to requirements.txt after verifying compatibility with Python 3.13 (or choose target Python 3.11/3.10 to maximize compatibility).

confusions.question: What exact connection URI pattern and port will code expect when reading DOCUMENTDB_URI?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect a MongoDB URI of the form `mongodb://<user>:<pass>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@` (TLS port 10255). The code will treat the env var as a drop-in `mongodb://` URI for Motor.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect to hardcode that pattern. The sample should treat DOCUMENTDB_URI as an opaque MongoDB connection string supplied by the cluster (portal / az), which for vCore clusters is typically a `mongodb+srv://...global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=...` SRV URI. The code must not assume port 10255 or that `.mongo.cosmos.azure.com` is used.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Legacy Cosmos DB Mongo API examples show `*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255`; vCore DocumentDB clusters publish SRV URIs and different host suffixes. The cold answer repeated the older pattern.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (older connection string examples)

confusions.build_risk: If code assumes a specific host/port the driver may mis-handle SRV URIs or fail to connect. The app code must take DOCUMENTDB_URI as-is and pass it to Motor without manual hostname/port parsing.
improvements: In README and sample code, show a `DOCUMENTDB_URI` placeholder and a one-liner: `client = AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'])` and warn not to hardcode host/port parsing.

information_gaps.title: OpenAI embedding model & dimensions
information_gaps.description: The sample needs a concrete embedding model choice (e.g., text-embedding-3-small, dimensions 1536) to pick index `dimensions` and to document vector storage. I searched Microsoft docs and agent skills; OpenAI model choice is external to DocumentDB docs and not provided by the provided materials.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset size & index tuning
information_gaps.description: The builder must choose how large the sample seed data should be (tiny demo vs realistic tens of thousands) because that drives the recommended vector index subtype (ivf/hnsw/diskann) and tuning (`lBuild`/`lSearch`/`maxDegree`). I inspected the documentdb-vector-search skill for guidance but the exact dataset size the author expects was not specified.

information_gaps.title: Affinity score formula (co-purchase count vs vector similarity)
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt requires ranking by an 'affinity score' but doesn't specify how to combine co-purchase frequency/count with embedding similarity. I searched the agent skills and docs (vector-search, data-modeling) and found guidance on storing counts and normalizing embeddings, but not a canonical mixing formula — the builder must pick and document one (e.g., weighted sum of normalized cosine similarity and log(count)).

information_gaps.title: Preferred Python target version
information_gaps.description: Inventory shows Python 3.13 on PATH, but Beanie compatibility and other dependencies may prefer 3.11/3.10. The docs/skills do not mandate a Python minor version; the builder must pick a target and pin dependency versions accordingly.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the `mongoClusters` resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) — do not assume `databaseAccounts` for vCore clusters; any IaC examples should target `mongoClusters`.

Treat DOCUMENTDB_URI as an opaque connection string: read it from env and pass it directly to Motor/Beanie (AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'])). Do not hardcode assumptions about port 10255 or host suffix patterns.

Create vector and full-text indexes using DocumentDB's search APIs (`createSearchIndexes` / `cosmosSearch`). Choose `vector-diskann` for M30+ or `vector-hnsw`/`vector-ivf` based on sample scale and store `embedding_model` and `dimensions` with each document.

For local development, use the DocumentDB gateway Docker image (gateway exposes Mongo protocol on port 10260) if you need local parity; otherwise verify against the live cluster per the run-environment.

Allow both native connection-string auth and Microsoft Entra ID in docs: show how to use DOCUMENTDB_URI for quickstart and note how to enable Entra/OIDC auth (`authConfig.allowedModes`) for production, linking to the Entra auth docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (the run-environment says use the provided live cluster). If you want to add an IaC & app deploy flow later, install azd via the official installer.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to run the sample against the provided cluster. If you plan to include IaC examples in the repo, add the Bicep CLI (`az bicep install`) or rely on `az deployment group` which has Bicep support.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary to build the sample against the existing cluster. If the team wants to include Terraform deploy examples, add Terraform to PATH or link to the AzAPI-based Terraform examples in docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python sample. If you provide .NET examples later, add dotnet SDK to PATH.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Adds convenience for manual, ad-hoc verification and quick index/collection checks. Install from MongoDB (download) or via package managers (macOS: `brew install mongosh`, npm: `npm i -g mongosh`) and then run `mongosh "$DOCUMENTDB_URI"` for quick checks.
